newsitem.title: USA: Marsh & McLennan deal to revive brokerage.
newsitem.headline: Marsh & McLennan deal to revive brokerage.

text.p: Marsh & McLennan Cos Inc's acquisition of Johnson & Higgins will jump-start its stagnant insurance brokerage operations and thrust it back into the position of world's largest insurance broker.
"This deal is arguably a strategic masterstroke for Marsh & McLennan," Smith Barney analyst Ron Frank said in comments to his sales force, a market source said on Wednesday.
With the deal, Marsh & McLennan can reclaim its position from Aon Corp as the largest insurance broker, as it bolsters earnings without sacrificing quality, analysts said.
Nutmeg Securities analyst Ira Zuckerman said Marsh & McLennan paid a full price for Johnson & Higgins, but the company should reap benefits quickly.

Marsh & McLennan said the proposed $1.8 billion acquisition would make a modest contribution to earnings in 1998 and a more substantial contribution by 2000. Earnings gains will be driven by annual cost savings of at least $150 million.
Analysts said they believed that estimate was low and that the company could save as much as twice that amount.
The deal comes at a time when insurance brokers are struggling to cope with stagnant or declining commissions. Insurance premium rates, the basis for commissions, have slumped during the past decade.
Indeed, in the fourth quarter of 1996, Marsh & McLennan's revenues from insurance services declined to about $449 million from about $475 million in the same quarter the previous year.
Other brokers have been forced to take action, too.
In December, Aon agreed to acquire Alexander & Alexander, and the industry may see other deals as well, analysts said.

Amid speculation about further consolidation, shares of Aruthur J. Gallagher & Co, an international insurance brokerage and risk-management services firm, rose 1-1/8, or about 3.5 percent, to close at 33 on Wednesday.
Marsh & McLennan said it was still in talks to buy St. Paul Cos Inc's London-based Minet brokerage but declined comment on whether it has talked with other brokers.
"We are always alert to the possibility of a combination that will be good for our clients, our staff and our shareholders," Marsh & McLennan Chief Executive A.J.C. Smith said.
In January, Marsh & McLennan purchased French insurance broker Compagnie Europeenne de Courtage d'Assurances et de Reassurances (CECAR).

Although Marsh & McLennan's highly regarded insurance brokerage business has had to contend with difficult market conditions, its Putnam asset-management business has been a successful money maker. The company said it was pleased with its Putnam business and plans to expand it, possibly through acquisitions.
The only possible negative aspect to the Johnson & Higgins deal is that it would reduce the proportion of Putnam's contribution to earnings, Smith Barney's Frank said, according to a market source.
